claims.text: Rapid quenching produces a dual-phase fcc/C14 microstructure in FeCoNiTi.
The fcc matrix in the rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi alloy is ferromagnetic.
The C14 Laves phase in FeCoNiTi is Ti-rich.
The fcc/C14 interface has crystallographic mismatch.
Ti segregates at the fcc/C14 interface.
Crystallographic mismatch and Ti segregation create a high-magnetic-anisotropy interfacial region.
Fe, Co, and Ni moments in the fcc phase couple antiferromagnetically to the Ti-rich C14 phase.
Antiferromagnetic coupling to the C14 phase reduces the net magnetic moment and saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
The C14/fcc phase boundaries are strong magnetic-domain-wall pinning sites.
Domain-wall pinning at the C14/fcc boundaries remains effective against thermal activation at 400 K.
C14-mediated pinning and magnetic anisotropy raise coercivity to approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
Dual-phase FeCoNiTi has lower saturation magnetization than single-phase fcc FeCoNi.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at approximately 100 Oe because their orbital moments are insufficient.
A sufficiently large C14 volume fraction is required to form a percolating network of domain-wall pinning sites.
Removing the C14 phase causes coercivity to revert to approximately 100 Oe.
The proposed mechanism requires the C14 phase to remain antiferromagnetic or weakly ferromagnetic at 400 K.
Interfacial coherence and Ti segregation vary with quenching rate and thereby affect the pinning force.
DFT with longitudinal spin-fluctuation corrections will be used to calculate the fcc spin density of states at the Fermi level and test for Ti-induced moment reduction.
Magnetic measurements on a C14-dominant, high-Ti alloy will be compared with dual-phase and single-phase fcc variants to isolate the C14 magnetic contribution.
